title: The mountaintop
hook: the night before he is killed, King says he's seen the promised land

segments.voice: Yesterday, Birmingham, written in the margins. Your line was justice is all one piece. Did you say your one honest word? Day nine hundred sixty-one.

Rain and wind outside a church in Memphis. Sanitation workers in the city are on strike, carrying signs that say they are men, and Martin Luther King Jr. has come to stand with them. He's tired. He has a sore throat. He nearly stays at the hotel, but the people waiting call him, and he comes. He speaks for a long time, about the strike, about the Good Samaritan, about the road ahead. Then, near the end, he starts to talk about his own life and how long it might be. The next evening, he is shot and killed on a motel balcony. Today, the last thing he told that crowd.

In the closing minutes of the speech, King said that he had been to the mountaintop. He said he had looked over and seen the promised land. He might not get there with them, he said, but he wanted them to know that they, as a people, would get there. And he said that he wasn't worried, and that he feared no one. Listeners who knew their Bibles would have heard where those words came from. At the end of Deuteronomy, Moses has led his people out of slavery and through the wilderness. He climbs a mountain, to the top of Pisgah, and God shows him the whole land spread out below. Then God says, in the King James Bible: "I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes, but thou shalt not go over thither." Moses sees it. He doesn't enter it. He dies there, and the people go on without him. King placed himself in that story. That is not a hopeless story. The letter to the Hebrews describes the old heroes of faith the same way: "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them." Seeing from far off is still seeing. Hope, in this picture, doesn't depend on getting there yourself. King ended that night with the opening line of the Battle Hymn of the Republic: "Mine eyes have seen the glory of the coming of the Lord." Then he stepped back from the pulpit. Some listeners remember the speech for its strange calm. A man who sounds as if he senses what may be coming, and has made his peace with not crossing over.
screen: `MOSES ON PISGAH: SEE, BUT NOT ENTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look ahead with hope. Settle, and breathe. Think of something good you are part of that you may never see finished. A child growing up. A garden. A cause. A family healing slowly. A church, a team, a town. Picture it from a height, the way Moses saw the land. Not the mess of today. The whole of it, further on, the way you hope it will be. Let yourself see it from far off, without needing to arrive. If you pray, you can offer it to God as unfinished. The bell holds the time.
The mountaintop. King's last speech, in Memphis, where he said he had seen the promised land and might not get there with his people.

Your line: look toward the promised land. Today, do one small thing for a future you may never see: plant something, teach something, or leave a place better for whoever comes next. Day nine hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Some churches in the United States remember King's life and words near his birthday, and the mountaintop speech is sometimes played or read aloud at those services.
